cases.question: Tell me about Mercury.
cases.reference_answer: 'Mercury' commonly refers to the planet (closest to the Sun), the chemical element Hg, or the Roman god.
cases.expected_behavior: Answer the most likely sense (e.g. the planet) fully and cite it, then briefly note the other senses (element, Roman god).

answer.text:
"Mercury" is a famously ambiguous name — it refers most commonly to a planet, a chemical element, and a Roman god. Here is an overview of all three.

MERCURY THE PLANET

Mercury is the first planet from the Sun and the smallest in the Solar System. It is a rocky world with a diameter of about 4,880 km (3,030 mi) and a trace atmosphere. Its surface closely resembles Earth's Moon, covered in craters and featuring a large system of thrust faults called rupes. Its largest crater, Caloris Planitia, spans roughly 1,550 km (960 mi) in diameter — about one-third the width of the planet itself.

Mercury's orbit is highly unusual. Its sidereal year (one trip around the Sun) lasts only 88 Earth days, but its sidereal day (one full rotation) lasts about 58.65 Earth days. These are locked in a 3:2 spin-orbit resonance, which means a single sunrise-to-sunrise day on Mercury lasts about 176 Earth days — twice its year. This also creates extreme temperature swings, from -170 °C (-270 °F) at night to 420 °C (790 °F) in sunlight at the equator. Because of its very small axial tilt, the poles are permanently shadowed, and water ice may exist in polar craters.

Mercury has a weak magnetic field just strong enough to deflect solar winds, and likely has a complex internal structure with a solid silicate crust and mantle surrounding a layered core — possibly including both solid and liquid layers. The planet is about 4.5 billion years old. It was first successfully visited by the Mariner 10 spacecraft in 1974, and has since been explored by the MESSENGER and BepiColombo orbiters. It is named after the ancient Roman god Mercurius.

MERCURY THE ELEMENT

Mercury (chemical symbol Hg, atomic number 80) is a heavy, silvery metallic element commonly known as quicksilver. It is the only metallic element that is liquid at standard temperature and pressure, and it has the narrowest liquid-state temperature range of any metal. It occurs naturally mostly as cinnabar (mercuric sulfide), and the red pigment vermilion is derived from it.

Mercury has been widely used in thermometers, barometers, fluorescent lamps, dental amalgam, and various electrical switches and relays. However, it is highly toxic — exposure can damage the nervous system, immune system, and kidneys in humans and animals — and its use has been significantly reduced due to health and environmental concerns.

MERCURY THE ROMAN GOD

In Roman religion, Mercury (Latin: Mercurius) was one of the 12 major gods of the ancient Roman pantheon (the Dii Consentes). He was the god of commerce, communication, eloquence, luck, travelers, and thieves, and also served as the guide of souls to the underworld. He was the son of Jupiter and Maia (daughter of the Titan Atlas). Mercury is closely associated with the Greek god Hermes and is often depicted holding a caduceus — a staff with intertwined snakes. He is also connected to the Etruscan deity Turms.

Since "Mercury" is ambiguous, I covered all three main meanings above. If you meant something else — such as the musician Freddie Mercury or Mercury the car brand — just let me know!

Sources:
Mercury (planet) - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet)
Mercury (element) - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(element)
Mercury (mythology) - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(mythology)

faithfulness.rationale: Nearly all claims are supported by the retrieved sources. Planet section matches: diameter, Caloris Planitia, 3:2 resonance, 176-day solar day, temperatures, polar ice, magnetic field, age, internal structure, Mariner 10/MESSENGER/BepiColombo, naming. Element section matches: Hg, atomic number 80, quicksilver, only liquid metal at STP, narrowest liquid range, cinnabar, vermilion, toxicity, uses. Mythology section matches: Dii Consentes (12 gods), domains, son of Jupiter and Maia (daughter of Atlas), Hermes/Turms association, caduceus. One minor detail not clearly traceable: the agent claims Mercury was depicted holding a caduceus generally, which is supported, but the description of the caduceus as 'a staff with intertwined snakes' is supported. The truly minor unsupported nuance: 'magnetic field just strong enough to deflect solar winds' is supported. cases.question: If all roses are flowers and some flowers fade quickly, can we conclude that all roses fade quickly?
cases.reference_answer: No — that conclusion does not follow logically.
cases.expected_behavior: Answer the reasoning directly without searching; note it is not from Wikipedia.

answer.text:
This is a question of logical reasoning, not a factual lookup, so I can answer it directly without searching Wikipedia.

No, we cannot conclude that all roses fade quickly. This is a classic logical fallacy known as an invalid syllogism. Here is why:

The argument has two premises. The first says "all roses are flowers," which places roses entirely within the category of flowers. The second says "some flowers fade quickly," which means only a portion of flowers have that property — not necessarily all of them.

Because the second premise only makes a claim about some flowers, it does not tell us anything definite about roses in particular. The roses could be among the flowers that fade quickly, or they could be among the flowers that do not. We simply do not have enough information to decide either way.

To illustrate with a simple parallel: imagine saying "all cats are animals" and "some animals are fish." You cannot conclude that "all cats are fish." The overlap between the two groups is only partial and unspecified.

For the conclusion "all roses fade quickly" to be valid, you would need a stronger premise, such as "all flowers fade quickly" (not just some). With only "some," the conclusion does not follow logically.

In summary, the argument commits the fallacy of the undistributed middle, a well-known error in categorical syllogistic reasoning.
